Flyto2 flyto-verification unauthenticated POST /run on :8344 (CVE-2026-67426 SSRF entry) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP POST to the /run endpoint of the flyto-verification service on TCP 8344 from non-loopback/remote sources. The shipped Dockerfile binds 0.0.0.0:8344 and /run has no auth dependency, so any remote POST /run is the unauthenticated entry point for the callback_url SSRF and runner-secret exfiltration chain. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete endpoint (POST /run) and the Dockerfile-shipped port 8344 (verification_service.py:363-364, Dockerfile.verification CMD). Restricting to external/remote sources leverages the fix guidance ('bind loopback by default') to separate attack traffic from legit internal callers. Corroborated against the GitLab advisory confirming the 0.0.0.0:8344 exposure. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/flyto-core/CVE-2026-67426/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-67426
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal verification jobs POSTing /run from an app tier reachable via a public NAT egress IP
  • Vulnerability scanners / ASM tools probing the /run path on 8344
  • Load-balancer or uptime health checks hitting /run
  • Developer testing the verification service from a bastion/VPN with a public source IP
Suppression filter
| where not(SourceIP in ("<known-healthcheck-ip>"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is external and not an expected internal caller; pull the full request (body should contain callback_url/workflowYaml) from app or proxy logs and check whether the host is running flyto-core <= 2.26.6. 2) Contain: rebind flyto-verification to loopback (or firewall 8344 to internal only), and rotate FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET immediately since it may already be exfiltrated. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2/UC3 — search for outbound connections from the verification host to 169.254.169.254 or to any public IP, and audit engine-callback authentications using the (now-possibly-leaked) runner secret.

| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort == 8344
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 8344
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/run"
| where isnotempty(SourceIP) and not(SourceIP startswith "10." or SourceIP startswith "192.168." or SourceIP startswith "172.16." or SourceIP startswith "127.")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

flyto-verification SSRF to cloud metadata IP (169.254.169.254) — runner-secret/IMDS theft AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts outbound connections from the flyto-verification runner (python/uvicorn/gunicorn/flyto-verification) to cloud instance-metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254, 100.100.100.200, metadata.google.internal). CVE-2026-67426's callback_url bypasses the target_allowed allowlist and SSRF guard, letting an attacker force the service to POST to the IMDS with a controlled body and harvest instance credentials. Rationale: The article explicitly names 'cloud-metadata IP' as an SSRF target; MITRE T1552.005 and Elastic's prebuilt IMDS-SSRF rule confirm 169.254.169.254 (plus Alibaba 100.100.100.200 / GCP metadata.google.internal) as the canonical endpoints. Scoping to the python/flyto-verification process removes legit cloud-agent IMDS calls, making a web-runner->IMDS connection a near-zero-FP signal. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005/ • https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/security/prebuilt-rules/rules/cross-platform/credential_access_web_server_cloud_imds_ssrf_request • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/flyto-core/CVE-2026-67426/
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate flyto workflow that intentionally targets an internal 169.254.x host as a callback (rare/misconfig)
  • Cloud SDK embedded in the same python venv making a genuine IMDSv2 token call for the app's own role
  • Security testing / red-team validation of the SSRF fix
  • Sidecar or observability agent sharing the process name 'python' reaching metadata for instance tags
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("flyto", "verification")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is the flyto-verification runner and capture the destination path/body; check IMDS access logs (if IMDSv2 enabled) for a token issuance from this host at the same time. 2) Contain: rotate FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET and any instance-role credentials that IMDS could have returned; enforce IMDSv2 (HttpTokens=required) and block 169.254.0.0/16 egress from the container; upgrade flyto-core to 2.26.7. 3) Hunt: search CloudTrail/AAD/GCP audit for use of the instance-role or managed-identity credentials from unexpected IPs shortly after this event, and check UC3 for the secret being POSTed to an external attacker host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("169.254.169.254", "100.100.100.200") or RemoteUrl has "metadata.google.internal"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python", "python3", "uvicorn", "gunicorn", "flyto-verification", "flyto")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("169.254.169.254", "100.100.100.200") or DstHostname has "metadata.google.internal"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

flyto-verification runner egress to external public host — FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET exfiltration AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the flyto-verification/python runner initiating outbound connections to public (non-RFC1918, non-link-local) destinations. Because callback_url is attacker-controlled and the service unconditionally attaches X-Internal-Key: $FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET, any egress from this backend runner to an arbitrary internet host is a candidate secret-exfiltration callback. Rationale: Grounded in the sink from the advisory: post_callback -> session.post(callback_url, headers={'X-Internal-Key': FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET}) (verification_service.py:330-335). A backend verification runner that is only supposed to call the internal engine should never egress to a public IP, so process-scoped public egress is a high-value exfiltration hunt for the leaked runner secret. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jx74-cqjv-2c67 • https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-67428
ATT&CKT1567 T1552
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate engine callback endpoint hosted on a public IP / SaaS domain rather than internal
  • Python dependency/package fetches (pip, telemetry SDKs) from the same runner venv
  • Outbound calls to a public webhook/notification service used by real workflows
  • CDN or object-storage uploads the workflow performs as designed
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !has "pypi.org" and RemoteUrl !has "pythonhosted.org"
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the public RemoteIP/RemoteUrl and compare against the documented internal engine callback host; if it is unknown/attacker-looking, capture the flow and any TLS SNI. 2) Contain: block egress from the flyto-verification container except to the known engine, rotate FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET, and upgrade to flyto-core 2.26.7. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 (inbound POST /run carrying that callback_url) and UC2 (IMDS access), and review engine-callback auth logs for forged authenticated callbacks using the leaked X-Internal-Key.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("flyto-verification", "flyto")) or (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python", "python3", "uvicorn", "gunicorn") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "flyto")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess", "ConnectionAttempt")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Count=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl
| order by FirstSeen desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OctLurk persistence: 'GoogleUpDate' scheduled task executing Videos\1.bat AIInstallation High
Hunts the OctLurk deployment technique where the actor creates a scheduled task named GoogleUpDate that runs, once, as SYSTEM, a batch script staged at C:\Users\<user>\Videos\1.bat. That batch script (MD5 6ecf84fb18f6747ed08d7598364d853a) creates the malicious service that side-loads the loader DLL. Article-specific because the task name masquerades as a Google updater but launches a .bat from the Videos folder — a combination legitimate updaters never use. Rationale: Anchors on two exact article strings: the task name 'GoogleUpDate' and the payload path '\Videos\1.bat' (MD5 6ecf84fb18f6747ed08d7598364d853a). A batch file in a media folder driven by a fake Google-update task is unique to this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/octlurk-and-silklurk-backdoors/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/new-backdoors-let-hackers-keylog/ • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Google Update tasks are named 'GoogleUpdateTaskMachine*' and run GoogleUpdate.exe from Program Files — never a .bat in Videos, so overlap is minimal
  • An admin scripting an ad-hoc scheduled task that happens to reference a file literally named 1.bat under a user profile
  • Software-deployment tooling (SCCM/Intune) staging batch scripts in unusual user folders
  • Red-team/pentest persistence tests mimicking updater task names
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","intunemanagementextension.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "GoogleUpdateTaskMachine")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the scheduled task XML (Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName GoogleUpDate) and the 1.bat contents; confirm the task runs as SYSTEM, once, and creates a service. Hash 1.bat against MD5 6ecf84fb18f6747ed08d7598364d853a. 2) Contain: Disable/delete the task, isolate the host, and block the loader DLL and its service (see the service-creation UC). 3) Hunt: Sweep the estate for the same task name and for the follow-on services (NgcCIntSvc, Cusrxsrv, etc.) and beacons to the OctLurk C2 domains.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "GoogleUpDate")
    or ProcessCommandLine has @"\Videos\1.bat"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe" and CommandLine has "GoogleUpDate")
    or CommandLine has "\\Videos\\1.bat"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OctLurk/LurkProxy service DLL side-load via RegisterService ServiceMain AIInstallation High
Hunts the service-based persistence where a batch script (1.bat / auto.bat) registers a Windows service whose ServiceMain registry value points to the 'RegisterService' export of a loader DLL (oleasapi.dll, msbasesysdc.dll). Detects both the anomalous ServiceMain=RegisterService registry write and the campaign's distinctive service names. Article-specific: legitimate svchost DLL services never name their entry point 'RegisterService'. Rationale: Uses the exact loader DLL names (oleasapi.dll, msbasesysdc.dll), the anomalous ServiceMain export 'RegisterService', and the clearly-malicious service names (NgcCIntSvc, Cusrxsrv, specitsrc, cmtastsvc). ServiceMain naming its entry point RegisterService is not a legitimate pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/octlurk-and-silklurk-backdoors/ • https://www.cryptika.com/new-backdoors-let-hackers-keylog-steal-passwords-and-control-government-computers/ • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1055
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A vendor product legitimately naming a service ServiceDll export 'RegisterService' (rare but possible for custom svchost DLL services)
  • Hyper-V integration services (vmic*) and PNRPHostSvc are legitimate names — excluded here to avoid FPs, only the non-standard names are matched
  • Endpoint agents that write to Services keys during install (match narrowed to the two loader DLL names)
  • Backup/imaging tools that re-create service registry keys during restore
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","trustedinstaller.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Open the flagged service registry key, note the ServiceDll path and hash the DLL (compare to oleasapi.dll 082d49ef9f14e6811d68c7e0e82e5069). Identify the parent process that wrote the key (1.bat/auto.bat/cmd.exe). 2) Contain: Stop and delete the service, quarantine the loader DLL, isolate the host — the loader reflectively injects the backdoor into memory so a memory capture before reboot is valuable. 3) Hunt: Search for the sibling service names across the fleet and for beacons to the campaign C2 (next UC); pull the batch scripts to find the admin credentials used for remote task/service creation.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\Services\"
| where (RegistryValueName =~ "ServiceMain" and RegistryValueData =~ "RegisterService")
    or (RegistryValueName =~ "ServiceDll" and RegistryValueData has_any ("oleasapi.dll","msbasesysdc.dll"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (7045, 4697)
| where ServiceName in~ ("NgcCIntSvc","Cusrxsrv","specitsrc","cmtastsvc")
    or ServiceFileName has_any ("oleasapi.dll","msbasesysdc.dll")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceStartType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OctLurk/SilkLurk/LurkProxy C2 beacon to campaign infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts network connections to the hard-coded OctLurk, SilkLurk and LurkProxy C2 domains and IP addresses over TLS/443 (and the LurkProxy connectivity pre-check to dns.ssentialserv.xyz -> 154.196.162.76). Article-specific: these are the exact backdoor domains/IPs published in the Kaspersky IOC set. Rationale: Exact FQDNs and IPs from the published IOC list, matched on full hostnames (not the parent dynamic-DNS providers gleeze.com/kozow.com) to avoid collateral. Includes the LurkProxy pre-check domain dns.ssentialserv.xyz -> 154.196.162.76. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/octlurk-and-silklurk-backdoors/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/new-backdoors-let-hackers-keylog/ • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • digital.leroymerlin.com resembles the legitimate Leroy Merlin retailer domain — verify the resolved IP against the IOC list before escalating on that hostname alone
  • Shared hosting / VPS IPs (Vultr/Choopa ranges like 95.179.x, 45.77.x) may later be reassigned to benign tenants — decays over time
  • Security scanners or threat-intel enrichment tools deliberately resolving IOC domains
  • An analyst workstation browsing to the IOCs during investigation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") or RemoteIP in (c2Ips)
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the initiating process for the connection (InitiatingProcessFileName) — expect svchost.exe hosting the malicious service, or a LurkProxy process. Confirm TLS/443 and beaconing cadence. 2) Contain: Block the domains/IPs at the proxy and perimeter firewall, isolate any beaconing host. 3) Hunt: For each host, pivot to the loader service and GoogleUpDate task UCs, and check for LurkProxy listening on port 64980 and follow-on tooling (fscan, secretsdump, Pandora RC agent).
let c2Domains = dynamic(["dns.multitoconference.com","tj.tajikistandip.com","fm01.clouddevicemetrics.com","confbase.mdpsupport.net","digital.leroymerlin.com","api2.annoyingremote.com","about.blsouqs.com","ssl.blsouqs.com","dns.ssentialserv.xyz","tyhbgtyuj.gleeze.com","wedfcvbn.gleeze.com","rgnojb.casacam.net","ctyuhjerf.kozow.com","uyhvfredc.accesscam.org","gycudore.kozow.com"]);
let c2Ips = dynamic(["45.138.157.165","154.196.162.76","95.179.210.138","45.77.136.228","95.179.141.26","45.32.152.50","212.11.39.138","195.86.120.2","154.196.187.73","45.61.149.112","64.7.198.130"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl in~ (c2Domains) or RemoteIP in (c2Ips)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2Domains = dynamic(["dns.multitoconference.com","tj.tajikistandip.com","fm01.clouddevicemetrics.com","confbase.mdpsupport.net","digital.leroymerlin.com","api2.annoyingremote.com","about.blsouqs.com","ssl.blsouqs.com","dns.ssentialserv.xyz","tyhbgtyuj.gleeze.com","wedfcvbn.gleeze.com","rgnojb.casacam.net","ctyuhjerf.kozow.com","uyhvfredc.accesscam.org","gycudore.kozow.com"]);
let c2Ips = dynamic(["45.138.157.165","154.196.162.76","95.179.210.138","45.77.136.228","95.179.141.26","45.32.152.50","212.11.39.138","195.86.120.2","154.196.187.73","45.61.149.112","64.7.198.130"]);
union
 (ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery in~ (c2Domains) | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, Src=SrcIpAddr, Indicator=DnsQuery, EvtType="DNS"),
 (ImNetworkSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DstIpAddr in (c2Ips) | project TimeGenerated, Host=SrcHostname, Src=SrcIpAddr, Indicator=DstIpAddr, DstPort=DstPortNumber, EvtType="NetConn")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OctLurk Command Shell plugin post-compromise recon cluster (chcp 1256 + session enum) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the OctLurk Command Shell plugin's post-compromise reconnaissance: it launches cmd.exe and runs chcp 1256 (Arabic code page), powershell $PSVersionTable, qwinsta, klist sessions and TASKLIST /V. Fires when three or more of these article-specific recon commands cluster on one host within an hour. The chcp 1256 switch is a strong differentiator tying the activity to this actor's Syria-targeting operations. Rationale: Anchors on the exact recon commands from the article's Command Shell plugin table (chcp 1256, qwinsta, klist sessions, TASKLIST /V, $PSVersionTable). chcp 1256 (Arabic code page) on a Central Asian government host is highly unusual; requiring 3+ distinct commands in an hour suppresses one-off admin use. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/new-backdoors-let-hackers-keylog/
ATT&CKT1614.001 T1033 T1057
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin or helpdesk running qwinsta/tasklist/klist during legitimate session or Kerberos troubleshooting
  • Logon scripts or monitoring agents that enumerate sessions and processes on a schedule
  • Legitimately Arabic-locale machines where chcp 1256 is set by the OS (rare in Central Asia targets)
  • Software inventory tooling querying $PSVersionTable during discovery
Suppression filter
| where Parents !has "mmc.exe" and not (Parents has "explorer.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Review the parent chain of the recon commands — OctLurk drives them via a cmd.exe launched by svchost.exe hosting the malicious service. Legitimate admin recon usually descends from an interactive shell/RDP session. 2) Contain: If the parent is a suspicious svchost/service, isolate the host and proceed to the service and C2 UCs. 3) Hunt: Look for follow-on credential access (secretsdump, browser password stealer), fscan network scanning, keylogger drops, and Pandora RC agent remote-access installs on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "chcp.com" and ProcessCommandLine has "1256")
    or FileName =~ "qwinsta.exe"
    or (FileName =~ "klist.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "sessions")
    or (FileName =~ "tasklist.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/V")
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "$PSVersionTable")
| summarize DistinctCmds = dcount(FileName), Cmds = make_set(ProcessCommandLine),
            Parents = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
            by DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where DistinctCmds >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\chcp.com" and CommandLine has "1256")
    or NewProcessName endswith "\\qwinsta.exe"
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\klist.exe" and CommandLine has "sessions")
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\tasklist.exe" and CommandLine has "/V")
    or (NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and CommandLine has "$PSVersionTable")
| summarize DistinctCmds = dcount(NewProcessName), Cmds = make_set(CommandLine),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctCmds >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 ((@Image:(*\\chcp.com OR *\\CHCP.COM) AND @CommandLine:*1256*) OR @Image:(*\\qwinsta.exe OR *\\QWINSTA.EXE) OR (@Image:(*\\klist.exe OR *\\KLIST.EXE) AND @CommandLine:*sessions*) OR (@Image:(*\\tasklist.exe OR *\\TASKLIST.EXE) AND @CommandLine:*\/V*) OR @CommandLine:*$PSVersionTable*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ((ImageFileName=/\\chcp\.com$/i AND CommandLine=/1256/) OR ImageFileName=/\\qwinsta\.exe$/i OR (ImageFileName=/\\klist\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/sessions/i) OR (ImageFileName=/\\tasklist\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/\s\/V/i) OR CommandLine=/\$PSVersionTable/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count(field=ImageFileName, distinct=true), as=distinct_cmds)
| distinct_cmds >= 3
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Processes.process) as commands dc(Processes.process_name) as distinct_cmds min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=chcp.com AND Processes.process="*1256*") OR Processes.process_name=qwinsta.exe OR (Processes.process_name=klist.exe AND Processes.process="*sessions*") OR (Processes.process_name=tasklist.exe AND Processes.process="*/V*") OR Processes.process="*$PSVersionTable*" by Processes.dest _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where distinct_cmds>=3
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Service install for persistence — sc.exe / new service registry write Installation High
Service install with binPath pointing to user-writeable path or LOLBin. Detects via process telemetry (sc.exe create) and registry (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\* writes).
ATT&CKT1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Registry DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "sc.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "create"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
// EventID 4697 is "Service installed" — direct signal, no cmdline-regex needed.
union
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4697
        | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName,
                  Detail = strcat("ServiceName=", ServiceName, " | Image=", ServiceFileName) ),
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4688
        | where Account !endswith "$"
        | where NewProcessName endswith "\sc.exe" and CommandLine has "create"
        | where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account,
                  Detail = strcat("4688 sc.exe create: ", CommandLine) )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1027

    category: process_creation
    product: windows

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Watering-hole exploit-script delivery from jshosting[.]me (AnySign4PC drive-by) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Exploited AnySign4PC.exe spawning child process or dropping DLL · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hackers Exploit AnySign4PC via Hacked Korean Sites to Install Backdoors Without
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SIGNBT/Gunra payload staging via net.tmp and inet.tmp · [LLM] COPPERHEDGE/SIGNBT C2 config in service-registry blobs + unusual service creation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] C2 / reverse-SSH-tunnel to 176.65.128[.]26 (Operation Double Barrel infra) · [LLM] Injected Microsoft process (SyncHost.exe / svchost.exe) making unexpected outbound connection · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Anti-forensic evidence destruction: SDelete / CCleaner + 4-char rename-then-delete · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Watering-hole exploit-script delivery from jshosting[.]me (AnySign4PC drive-by) AIDelivery High
Hunts endpoint contact with jshosting[.]me, the domain AhnLab/KISA attribute to distribution of the version-specific AnySign4PC exploit scripts in both the state-sponsored and Gunra chains. Because the exploit runs with no download prompt, the DNS/HTTP callout to this domain is often the earliest host-visible signal of the drive-by. Rationale: jshosting[.]me is a hard IOC confirmed by AhnLab as the exploit-script distribution domain shared by both the espionage and Gunra intrusions; a corporate host resolving it is high-fidelity given it is not a legitimate service. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/94696/ • https://image.ahnlab.com/atip/content/file/20260730/%5BAhnLab%5DOperation%20Double%20Barrel(ENG)(2026.07.30).pdf
ATT&CKT1189 T1608.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or SOC analyst detonating the sample in a sandbox that egresses through the corporate resolver
  • Threat-intel enrichment/crawler tooling actively resolving IOC domains
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ appliance logging the query as it blocks it (verify answer is sinkhole IP)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess making the callout — a browser process is consistent with the watering-hole drive-by; confirm the user visited a Korean news/healthcare/education site immediately prior. 2) Contain: block jshosting[.]me at proxy/DNS, isolate the host, and snapshot AnySign4PC version (flag 1.1.4.4–1.1.4.6). 3) Hunt: on the same host look for AnySign4PC.exe spawning children/writing DLLs, injection into svchost.exe/SyncHost.exe, and outbound to 176.65.128[.]26.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "jshosting.me" or RemoteUrl endswith ".jshosting.me"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "jshosting.me"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exploited AnySign4PC.exe spawning child process or dropping DLL AIExploitation High
Hunts the post-exploitation moment where the buffer-overflow in AnySign4PC.exe (Hancom Secure e-signature client) forces the signed process to spawn a child or write a DLL to disk with no user interaction. A certificate-signing client legitimately never spawns interpreters/LOLBins or drops DLLs, so either behaviour from AnySign4PC.exe is anomalous. Rationale: AnySign4PC.exe is the exact exploited binary named by ENKI/KISA; a signing client spawning children or dropping DLLs is behaviourally impossible in benign use, matching Plainbit's 'generated an error and created a malicious DLL without a download prompt'. Cross-checked against: • https://www.enki.co.kr/en/media-center/blog/joint-cybersecurity-advisory-watering-hole-malware-analysis • https://www.file.net/process/anysign4pc.exe.html
ATT&CKT1203 T1055 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AnySign4PC auto-update spawning its own updater/installer (AnySignUpdate.exe)
  • Crash-handler WerFault.exe launched by AnySign4PC after a benign fault
  • Vendor troubleshooting tool bundled with AnySign4PC launching a helper
  • EDR/AV telemetry stub injected into AnySign4PC being recorded as a child
Suppression filter
| where FileName !in~ ("AnySignUpdate.exe","AnySignSetup.exe") and not (FileName =~ "WerFault.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "-p")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child process command line and any dropped DLL path/hash; a LOLBin (rundll32/regsvr32) child or a DLL written to ProgramData/Temp is a strong true positive. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture memory (backdoor decrypts stages in memory and may be disk-absent), and record AnySign4PC version. 3) Hunt: pivot to svchost.exe/SyncHost.exe injection, net.tmp/inet.tmp artifacts, service-registry blobs, and C2 to 176.65.128[.]26 on the same device.
let ProcSpawn = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "AnySign4PC.exe"
| where FileName !in~ ("AnySign4PC.exe","AnySignUpdate.exe","conhost.exe","WerFault.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Signal="ChildProcess", InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256;
let DllDrop = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "AnySign4PC.exe"
| where ActionType == "FileCreated" and FileName endswith ".dll"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Signal="DllDrop", InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256;
ProcSpawn | union DllDrop
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\AnySign4PC.exe"
| where NewProcessName !endswith "\\AnySign4PC.exe" and NewProcessName !endswith "\\conhost.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

C2 / reverse-SSH-tunnel to 176.65.128[.]26 (Operation Double Barrel infra) AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any outbound connection to 176.65.128[.]26, the reverse-tunnelling address AhnLab confirms was reused across both the state-sponsored SIGNBT/COPPERHEDGE chain and the Gunra ransomware chain. Any egress to this fixed IP from a corporate host is a high-confidence compromise indicator. Rationale: 176.65.128[.]26 is a fixed IOC that AhnLab confirms as the reverse-tunnelling address shared across both operations — a rare dual-corroborated hard indicator that warrants direct alerting. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/94696/ • https://www.rescana.com/post/lazarus-group-exploits-anysign4pc-zero-day-to-target-south-korean-financial-sector-via-drive-by-attacks
ATT&CKT1572 T1071 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel validation traffic or IOC scanner probing the IP from a security appliance
  • Firewall logging the connection as denied (check DeviceAction=blocked before escalating)
  • Shared hosting rebind — verify the IP is still attacker-controlled at alert time
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("nessus.exe","nmap.exe") and DeviceName !has "scanner"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — svchost.exe/SyncHost.exe or an unsigned binary reaching this IP is an immediate true positive; note the port (SSH/reverse-tunnel often 22/443). 2) Contain: block the IP org-wide, isolate the host, and preserve volatile memory before the loader's self-protection wipes disk artifacts. 3) Hunt: enumerate all internal hosts that contacted the IP, and on each check for Mimikatz/NLBrute, RDP fan-out, and service-registry C2 blobs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "176.65.128.26"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "176.65.128.26"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Injected Microsoft process (SyncHost.exe / svchost.exe) making unexpected outbound connection AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the SIGNBT/COPPERHEDGE post-injection C2 pattern where shellcode is injected into legitimate SyncHost.exe or svchost.exe which then beacons out. SyncHost.exe reaching the public internet is inherently anomalous, and svchost.exe egress to the known C2 is a direct hit — both are the article's named injection targets in the espionage and Gunra chains. Rationale: The article and corroborating AhnLab report name svchost.exe and SyncHost.exe as the specific injection targets; SyncHost.exe public egress is behaviourally rare, and svchost.exe to the named C2 IP scopes the noisy svchost case to a hard indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/94696/ • https://image.ahnlab.com/atip/content/file/20260730/%5BAhnLab%5DOperation%20Double%20Barrel(ENG)(2026.07.30).pdf
ATT&CKT1055.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SyncHost.exe legitimately syncing UWP/Mail-Calendar app data to Microsoft cloud endpoints (filter *.microsoft.com)
  • svchost.exe Windows Update / telemetry to Microsoft IP ranges (excluded via 20.* and MS domains)
  • Third-party sync client mis-named synchost.exe
  • Proxy/NAT collapsing many hosts behind one svchost egress record
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !endswith ".microsoft.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".live.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".office.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the remote IP is non-Microsoft; a SyncHost.exe connection to an unfamiliar VPS or the C2 IP is a true positive — pull the parent and any CreateRemoteThread (Sysmon 8) targeting the process. 2) Contain: isolate the host and capture memory before the in-memory PE is wiped. 3) Hunt: check the same host for AnySign4PC exploitation, encrypted service-registry C2 blobs, and reverse-tunnel egress to 176.65.128[.]26.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "SyncHost.exe" and RemoteIPType == "Public")
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe" and RemoteIP == "176.65.128.26")
| where RemoteIP !startswith "20." and RemoteUrl !endswith ".microsoft.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".windowsupdate.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (DstIpAddr == "176.65.128.26") or (tolower(tostring(split(SrcHostname,"\\")[-1])) == "synchost.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SIGNBT/Gunra payload staging via net.tmp and inet.tmp AIInstallation High
Hunts creation or execution of the payload files net.tmp and inet.tmp — filenames AhnLab confirms were reused across both the state-sponsored and Gunra chains, with net.tmp invoked with a GUID-format argument. Detects both the file drop and the rundll32/loader execution referencing these temp payloads. Rationale: net.tmp and inet.tmp are exact malware filenames AhnLab confirms across both operations, with net.tmp carrying a GUID-format argument; matching them in command lines and file drops is high-fidelity and rarely benign. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/94696/ • https://image.ahnlab.com/atip/content/file/20260730/%5BAhnLab%5DOperation%20Double%20Barrel(ENG)(2026.07.30).pdf
ATT&CKT1105 T1218.011 T1027.009
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate installer or app that happens to write a temp file literally named net.tmp/inet.tmp (rare; verify parent and path)
  • Network-config tooling logging to a *net.tmp scratch file
  • Backup/AV quarantine renaming a file to net.tmp coincidentally
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","svchost.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the file hash and the full command line — a GUID argument passed to net.tmp via rundll32/a loader is a strong true positive; the loader may side-load a DLL. 2) Contain: isolate the host and image memory (files may be deleted post-load and restored only at clean shutdown with a different hash). 3) Hunt: correlate with AnySign4PC exploitation, service-registry C2 blobs, and 176.65.128[.]26 egress; the same filenames appearing elsewhere may indicate the Gunra pre-ransomware stage.
let Drops = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("net.tmp","inet.tmp")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal="FileCreate", FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256;
let Exec = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("net.tmp","inet.tmp")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal="Exec", FileName, FolderPath=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256;
Drops | union Exec
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "net.tmp" or CommandLine has "inet.tmp"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

COPPERHEDGE/SIGNBT C2 config in service-registry blobs + unusual service creation AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the article's named persistence/C2-storage pattern: backdoors that read command-and-control information from encrypted blobs stored under service-registry entries, paired with unusual service creation. Flags registry value writes to CurrentControlSet\Services by non-installer processes and services whose ImagePath points at ProgramData/Temp/AppData. Rationale: The article and AhnLab explicitly recommend hunting 'encrypted data stored under service-registry entries' and 'unusual service creation'; scoping registry writes to CurrentControlSet\Services by non-installer processes and services running from ProgramData/Temp targets that exact tradecraft. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/94696/ • https://image.ahnlab.com/atip/content/file/20260730/%5BAhnLab%5DOperation%20Double%20Barrel(ENG)(2026.07.30).pdf
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1112 T1027.011
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry Endpoint.Services
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate driver/service installers writing binary config under Services keys via a non-standard installer
  • EDR/AV agents storing encrypted config blobs under their own service key
  • Backup or management agents installed from ProgramData with a service entry
  • GPO/SCCM software deployment creating services from staging paths
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !endswith "setup.exe" and RegistryKey !has "Sense" and RegistryKey !has "WinDefend"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process and the service ImagePath — a rundll32/unsigned binary writing a REG_BINARY blob under a Services key, or a service pointing at Temp/ProgramData, is a true positive. 2) Contain: isolate the host, export the registry blob for offline decryption, and disable the rogue service. 3) Hunt: extract C2 from the decrypted blob and sweep for egress to those IPs plus 176.65.128[.]26, and check for svchost/SyncHost injection on the same host.
let SvcRegBlob = DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentControlSet\Services\"
| where RegistryValueType == "Binary"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("services.exe","svchost.exe","msiexec.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","poqexec.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal="SvcRegBlob", RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
let SvcInstall = DeviceEvents

Anti-forensic evidence destruction: SDelete / CCleaner + 4-char rename-then-delete AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the article's named anti-forensic routine: renaming malicious files to random four-character names before deletion, with additional wiping via SDelete and CCleaner observed by Plainbit. Detects SDelete/CCleaner execution and the rename-to-4-char-name-then-delete file sequence. Rationale: Plainbit specifically observed SDelete and CCleaner used for evidence destruction, and AhnLab documented the rename-to-random-4-char-name-before-delete routine; combining the named tools with the rename/delete file pattern targets this exact anti-forensic tradecraft. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/94696/ • https://image.ahnlab.com/atip/content/file/20260730/%5BAhnLab%5DOperation%20Double%20Barrel(ENG)(2026.07.30).pdf
ATT&CKT1070.004 T1485 T1070.009
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin using SDelete legitimately to securely wipe free space or decommission a disk
  • IT running CCleaner as a sanctioned cleanup/maintenance tool
  • Software installers creating short temp filenames that get renamed/deleted normally
  • Backup software renaming files to short hashes during dedup
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccleaner.exe","CCUpdate.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Program Files") and AccountName !in~ ("itadmin","backupsvc")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check who/what launched the wiper — SDelete/CCleaner run by a non-admin user, a service account, or a process descended from AnySign4PC/svchost is a true positive; correlate rename-to-4-char events on the same host and time window. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately (evidence is being destroyed) and preserve any remaining volatile memory and MFT. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same host's exploitation, injection, and C2 indicators before artifacts are gone, and check for lateral movement (RDP, NLBrute) to other hosts.
let Wipers = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("sdelete.exe","sdelete64.exe","CCleaner.exe","CCleaner64.exe")
     or (ProcessCommandLine has "sdelete" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-p","-s","-nobanner"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Signal="WiperExec", FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName;
let RenameWipe = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileRenamed"
| where FileName matches regex @"^[A-Za-z0-9]{4}(\.[A-Za-z0-9]{1,4})?$"
| where PreviousFileName endswith ".dll" or PreviousFileName endswith ".tmp" or PreviousFileName endswith ".exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Signal="RenameToRandom", FileName, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName=PreviousFileName;
Wipers | union RenameWipe
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("sdelete.exe","sdelete64.exe","CCleaner.exe","CCleaner64.exe")
     or (CommandLine has "sdelete" and CommandLine has_any ("-p","-nobanner"))
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010

SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc
